newsitem.title: USA: Officials survey storm damage in Michigan.
newsitem.headline: Officials survey storm damage in Michigan.

text.p: Teams of state, federal and insurance company officials Monday sifted through damage wrought by last week's violent storms and tornadoes across Michigan to prepare an application for disaster relief funds.
Detroit area residents and volunteers continued the painful process of rebuilding homes and businesses shattered by the wave of storms on July 2, which have been blamed for up to 16 deaths.

Gov. John Engler declared Oakland, Macomb and Genesee counties in southeastern Michigan as state disaster areas, adding to disaster proclamations for Wayne County and the city of Detroit last week. Engler also authorized the Michigan National Guard to help cleanup efforts in Detroit and Wayne County.

Officials from the Federal Emergency Management Agency went from house to house in the hardest hit areas in Highland Park and Hamtramck, Mich. -- inner city enclaves surrounded by Detroit -- to assess damage.

Data collected by the agency will be submitted to President Clinton later this week, who will decide whether to offer disaster relief funds, such as low-interest loans or grants to help people rebuild homes.
"We can't possibly replace everything that you've lost," said FEMA spokeswoman Linda Sacia. "What FEMA's program is, is essentially housing needs, which is basic."

According to FEMA, initial reports indicated that at least 93 homes were destroyed and 400 were damaged by the storms. More than 100 businesses also sustained damage, as did hundreds of acres of farmland. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Farm Service Agency will survey crop damage in 10 Michigan counties.
Michigan State police estimate damage to public buildings at more than $135 million, a number officials expect to rise sharply.

The storms knocked out electrical power to about 350,000 customers, and by midday Monday, service had been restored to only about 5,000 customers in the hardest-hit areas, said Detroit Edison Co. spokeswoman Mary Kay Bean.
"Our electrical system was pretty much brought down to the ground. We had to clear debris out of the way, put up all new poles and put in new transformers," Bean said.
The utility brought in about 500 linemen from Illinois, Indiana and elsewhere in Michigan to help with the rebuilding effort.
But many heavily damaged homes cannot be reconnected to electrical power until internal damage is repaired, Bean said.
